paragraphs: The heat came early to Chang’an that summer. A sudden storm swept down at midday, sending water coursing along Vermilion Bird Avenue; by evening, a close, damp warmth was rising again from the joints between the paving stones. A seller of ice pushed his cart home from the western market, his wares more than half melted. It was then that an urgent dispatch from Beidi entered the city.

The report said Fu Luo had read a secret edict aloud to his camps, calling on the old retainers of the imperial clan to march on the capital and “purge the traitors beside the throne.” He had not openly declared rebellion. The seal on his official residence still identified him as Duke of Beihai, and the banners in his army still bore Qin’s name. Yet a strip of white cloth had been tied to the corner of each Qin flag, while Murong Chui, Quan Yi, and Fu Rong were denounced as petty men holding the Heavenly King hostage.

One figure in the report held Quan Yi’s brush suspended for half a day. Fu Luo’s army claimed to number thirty thousand, but those verified as capable of fighting amounted to perhaps eighteen thousand. The others were hurried recruits or men counted under borrowed household standards. Estate horsemen and former retainers continued to join on the march south. The number thirty thousand was like a leather bag swollen with wind; viewed from far enough away, it might indeed have looked like thirty thousand men.

Fu Jian listened to the report in his hall without becoming angry. He ordered the replies from seven frontier garrisons laid out by date. Two had answered Fu Luo’s call; three had shut their gates against all messengers; the remaining two were holding grain wagons and refusing to release them. The road from Beidi to Chang’an began to take on a more substantial color on the map.

His ministers urged him to move his court to Tong Pass. Its approaches were naturally defensible, and the armies east of the pass could be summoned to reinforce him. Once the emperor left Chang’an, Fu Luo’s claim that he had come to “protect the sovereign” would be emptied of meaning.
Fu Jian looked toward the Crown Prince. “Hong’er, what do you think?”

Fu Hong rolled up the garrisons' replies. His voice was a little strained. “If Your Majesty’s safety alone mattered, going east would be best. But the Duke of Beihai says you have fallen into the hands of surrendered ministers. If General Murong escorts you out of the city, people will hear only that the Heavenly King has been taken away. Even garrisons that have refused to join Fu Luo might then raise white banners.”
“You want us to hold the city?”
“I would not dare promise that we can hold it.”

Fu Jian studied his son. Fu Hong had made no grand declaration to conceal his fear, and that steadied the father’s mind. “No gate of Chang’an is to be opened for flight. Those with fields shall go on farming; those with shops shall keep them open. No gate is to change its guard upon the authority of one piece of paper. If a gate must be shut, three offices must verify the order together.”

Then he instructed Quan Yi to bring him the market price of grain and the granaries' reserves the following day. The rebel army had not yet arrived, but people were already rushing to buy food. In the western market a shi of millet cost thirty percent more than it had two days earlier. Rich families loaded gold and silver into carts; the poor shouldered half a sack of flour, afraid there would be none to buy tomorrow. The people of Chang’an had not waited for an edict granting them permission to be frightened.

Murong Chui came from the eastern camp with traces of Hexi sand still caught in his traveling cloak. After examining the city plan, he put a finger on Zhangcheng Gate. “Everyone will guard the northern gates against an army coming down from the north. This one opens onto estates and old storehouses. There are many tracks beyond the wall. If somebody first delivers a relief-of-guard order here, the advance guard will dare probe the entrance with fewer than a hundred horsemen.”

Fu Hong asked whether the garrison should be strengthened. Murong first asked who commanded the gate, who held the keys, and who checked the orders. He noted three names in his palm, then indicated the eastern and northern encampments. “I shall keep the main army outside. Two battalions inside will be enough. If we march everyone into the wards, the people will think we intend to slaughter the Di clansmen before the rebels arrive.”
Fu Jian turned his gaze to Yao Chang.

Yao had been ordered to guard the palace gates. He said the imperial granary lay to the southwest and that cutting its supply route would be disastrous. He volunteered to secure the storehouses with the Right Guard. Fu Hong added a condition: if fire broke out anywhere, no palace guard unit was to abandon its post in full. Any emergency change of guard at palace or city gates required the presence of the city-gate commandant, a Guard officer, and a Secretariat registrar, who would verify the order together. Yao did not object. He smiled. “The Crown Prince has thought of everything. I shall see that my men learn it by heart.”

Two days later, the hay stores west of the city caught fire. The flames were put out quickly; no one died that night. The next day the armory workshops burned, destroying bow racks and arrow shafts. On the third night a sheet of red flame rose above an oil shop in the eastern market, blackening and curling the sheepskins hung beneath its eaves. The shopkeeper knelt among the ruins, explaining that somebody had broken a hole in the rear wall large enough to drag a jar of oil through. Officers of the Judicial Commandant followed footprints as far as the mouth of the lane, where the rain had already washed the marks away.

Fu Hong summoned the ward elders. He did not begin by discussing how rebels were to be arrested. He asked how women and children could escape when the fires started. He ordered each ward to keep buckets, wet felts, and axes for breaking down walls, and forbade any single person from holding the only gate key. He marked routes to wells and open courtyards. Someone warned that locking the wards by night might trap innocent people in the flames. Fu Hong listened for a long time. Then he struck out four words from his original order—WARD GATES MUST NOT BE OPENED—and replaced them with: IN CASE OF FIRE, OPEN THE EMERGENCY PASSAGE; SOUND THE DRUM BEFORE OPENING; POST MEN TO RECEIVE THOSE FLEEING ON BOTH SIDES.

The Secretariat officials were surprised. In the past the Crown Prince had seldom changed his mind. Lately he had begun to admit, in front of other people, when his first instruction had been insufficient. “A gate is guarded to keep people alive,” he said, “not to let them die behind it.”

In the western market lived an old blacksmith surnamed Liu who made iron shoes for horses. His son had marched with the First Battalion six months before and had not returned. Only his daughter-in-law and a four-year-old grandchild remained at home. When the ward elder came with his men to explain fire precautions, the old smith grew impatient and threw an axe outside. “If the rebels come, who’ll stop them? Best seize the grain while you can.” His daughter-in-law picked up the axe and silently filled the water jar. That night the old smith could not know that this jar would save the lives of his neighbors.

Fu Luo sent cavalry ahead of his main army, several days' ride in front of it, to slip south along the tracks between the fields. Their leader was Fu Jian, a clan officer from the old imperial camps who was accustomed to swift raids. His name was pronounced like the Heavenly King’s, though written differently. Several others traveling with him knew the routes to the storehouses southwest of Chang’an. They numbered only seven or eight hundred. All had removed their standards and muffled their horses' hooves in cloth. They rode by night and rested by day, waiting for word from Zhangcheng Gate. Their commander said no civilians need be killed: once they reached the palace, they would merely ask the Heavenly King to show himself. An old soldier beside him asked, “And if the Heavenly King tells us to our faces that we are rebels?” The commander’s expression darkened. “The Duke of Beihai will explain it when he comes.”

Soon after the second watch, fire broke out almost simultaneously in three storehouses southwest of Chang’an. Hemp sacks outside the imperial granary had been soaked in burning oil; red tongues of flame licked along the eaves. A grain house in the north was also set alight, and the armory in the east sounded the alarm drums. Hundreds of household doors flew open together. Dogs barked, people screamed and wept. Cries that the northern gate had fallen and the Heavenly King had been murdered ran down the lanes. Some of those carrying the news fled so quickly they lost their shoes.

Fu Hong had scarcely put on his armor when he ordered three fire-signal drums raised outside the palace gate. Each district was to beat a different rhythm. If troops heard a cry that the palace had fallen, they were to listen first for the drums and not abandon their posts without orders. He sent the Secretariat’s available water carriers to the imperial granary and instructed the ward elders to lead old people and children toward the wells along familiar paths, before crowds could trample one another at the gates.

An urgent report now came from the Right Guard: Yao Chang had taken a detachment to save the imperial granary, drawing men away from both the northern and western palace gates. Fu Hong felt a chill. He asked the messenger, “Did His Majesty order him to go?”
“He said only that the imperial granary must not be lost.”

“No one disputes the importance of the granary.” Fu Hong sent another order through the Secretariat. “Restore the palace gate guards to their full strength at once. If the Right Guard is already fighting the fire, have the granary troops in the city relieve them. No more palace guards are to be sent.”
But commands traveled more slowly than fire in the night.

Beneath Zhangcheng Gate, an officer carrying a Right Guard token claimed to have an emergency order relieving the existing garrison, which was to hurry to the western granaries. Han Shou, the gate commandant, had defended Chang’an’s old walls when he was young. He knew little of the twists of written orders, but he knew that a gate once opened could not easily be closed. He stared at the visitor. “Where is Registrar Zhang Chong?”
“He has gone to the granary fire. His signature is here.”
“If he doesn’t come, my men don’t leave.”

The officer leaned close and lowered his voice. If the western granaries were lost, he said, no soldier or civilian in the city would have grain tomorrow. Han Shou asked, “Then why aren’t you out saving the grain? Why have you come at midnight to open my gate?”

The man’s expression shifted. A little later, two hundred soldiers wearing Right Guard armor did indeed come to relieve the watch. Han Shou refused to withdraw all his men. He allowed only half the garrison to rotate out and ordered his deputy to keep hold of the gate winch. The newcomers brushed shoulders with the old defenders upon the wall. The wooden steps were slippery from the rain; a man stumbled and his armor plates clattered together.

Then a knock came from outside the gate: three long strokes and two short ones. One of the new soldiers spun and ran for the winch. Han Shou shouted and seized him by the collar. A blade flashed from behind and to one side; he felt a sudden heat at his throat and saw the lamp knocked from his own hand. Burning oil spilled across the stone steps, flowering red for an instant.
When Han Shou fell, his fist was still closed upon the man’s sash.

The winch turned; the heavy leaves of the gate parted by a narrow crack. Horsemen waiting outside forced their way through and cut the ropes securing the barriers in the passage. The old defenders on the walls threw themselves against the doors from both sides. A soldier pierced by an arrow braced his shoulder against the gate pivot until another could take his place. The gate never opened fully. Only the rebel advance guard broke through with Fu Jian; those behind it found themselves shut out and fled back toward the fields.

Fu Jian did not wait for the rest. His men rushed along the western street toward the palace, crying, “By imperial edict, we have come to protect the sovereign!” They fired stacks of wood beside the road, hoping to draw out their allies within the city. White cloth did appear above several doors. But the thousands he had expected to rally to him did not emerge. Most ward gates were barred; wells were guarded; wagon bodies, their wheels removed, lay crosswise in the streets. At each turn a horse found itself stopped by a wagon shaft.

At the gate of Xuanping Ward, the crowd nearly crushed itself in panic. A woman carrying a child was knocked down; the little one rolled from her arms and screamed. When the Crown Prince arrived, ward soldiers were bracing the gate with long poles while people on both sides hurled curses at each other. He climbed down to investigate. There was no fire in the ward; the terror had begun with a rumor that rebels were in the next street. He ordered two guards to remain at the gate and a narrow lane beside the well to be opened so the old, the women, and the children could escape. The main ward gate was not to be thrown open for the crowd to rush through.

Someone hurled a stone at his carriage. His attendants drew their swords to charge into the crowd, but Fu Hong shouted them back. The ward elder, his forehead bloodied by another stone, was still standing before the gate. Panting, he called, “Your Highness, what if the fire reaches us?”

“Go toward the well. Pull down the wooden sheds joining one roof to another. Save the people first, then the goods. If the wind turns south, beat the drum three times, and I’ll have the neighboring ward receive you.”

The woman in the crowd finally gathered her child back into her arms. She did not kneel to thank the Crown Prince. She merely wiped her face, tightened her belt, and went back the way she had come. Fu Hong saw the muddy footprint across her back, left by someone who had trampled her. He thought suddenly that even if this order to hold the wards saved Chang’an, many people might hate him for it for years to come.

At the northwest corner of the palace, Fu Jian climbed the watchtower in armor. Smoke rose highest from the imperial granary. Toward Zhangcheng Gate a winding thread of torches was moving forward. His attendants once more urged him to withdraw to the eastern camp. He made no reply. Instead he ordered every lamp in Weiyang Palace lit and the banner of the Heavenly King raised high. Above the ward walls, the first thing people had seen was fire. Now they saw the Qin banner standing above the flames.
“His Majesty is in the palace!” voices shouted through the lanes.

Fu Jian heard the cries and drove his men faster. He promised that once inside the palace he would open the court and allow every veteran Di commander to present his grievances before the throne. But a Di military officer blocking the street lifted his shield and asked, “If His Majesty truly summoned you, why isn’t the Crown Prince waiting to welcome you at the palace gate?”
Fu Jian held up his sealed edict. “The Crown Prince has been deceived by traitors!”
“And the palace guards?”
“They’ve been deceived as well!”
The officer laughed in fury. “So in all of Chang’an, yours is the only household whose seal still knows the Heavenly King!”

He ordered two empty wagons dragged across the road. Before his front rank could level their spears, the riders charged. Horses smashed breastfirst into the timber with a terrible cracking. Both sides shouted the numbers of Qin units. After the first volley of arrows, no one could tell which battalion’s name was being cried.

In the eastern camp, Murong Chui heard the red beacon from Zhangcheng Gate and at last ordered the men to arm. The Di infantry looked uneasy; the Xianbei cavalry spoke even less than usual. Some believed that, because an imperial clansman had rebelled, the Qin court would offer up the Xianbei as the first victims. Others still remembered what Di troops had done when they entered the fallen Yan capital. Murong made no stirring address. He merely had the military law officer read the prohibitions: no entering private houses to search for people; no taking property; no killing anyone who had laid down his weapons. Anyone using the old tribal banners to call men of his own people together would be executed.
At the end, he looked over their faces. “I saw you save each other in the snow country of Dai. Tonight this is our own city. Once you pass its gates, don’t leave people wondering why you’ve come.”

The mixed central army entered by the eastern gate in good order: Di infantry bearing shields, Xianbei cavalry leading their horses, Han crossbowmen pushing barriers before them. Mounted troops could not gallop through such narrow streets, so Murong ordered every rider to dismount. When Qiang archers climbed onto a roof, they first helped the widow who lived beneath it into a neighboring house, and only then strung their bows to hold the lane.

The rebels fought their way to the approaches of the palace. Only two streets separated them from the banner of the Heavenly King. Fu Jian ordered fires lit to halt their pursuers, but another body of Right Guard soldiers appeared from the direction of the imperial granary. Smoke blackened Yao Chang’s armor. His men were carrying several granary soldiers who had been burned. They truly had fought the fires, and truly had saved several granary doors from the flames.
the rebel captain recognized Yao Chang and pulled on his reins. Incredulity spread across his face. “General Yao, you told us before—”

The rest of his words were drowned by the hiss of arrows. One struck his shoulder armor. He still tried to shout, but a spear brought down his horse. Right Guard soldiers closed in and dragged him clear of the animal. Yao rode forward and, seeing him still struggling, lifted one hand. “Don’t let him rush the palace again.”

The blade fell with terrible speed. The rebel captain Fu Jian died with his eyes open. Several officers who had already thrown away their weapons fell beside him. Murong Chui arrived and shouted for prisoners to be taken alive. Only when Yao raised his hand again did the killing stop.
“The man was bound,” Murong demanded from the saddle. “Why wasn’t he taken to the Judicial Commandant?”

Yao looked toward the flames at the palace gate. “When the general arrived, men were still killing each other in the streets. My soldiers were wounded. We did not have the leisure you seem to have had.”
“What were his last words?”
“Whose?”
“the rebel captain’s.”
“I couldn’t hear them.”

Murong leaned down to inspect the wounds. The arrow through the shoulder armor had not been mortal; the cut across the throat was almost clean. Behind Yao Chang, the bodyguards sheathed their blades together, as if nothing at all had happened. Murong asked no further questions. He ordered his military law officers to register the weapons, the prisoners, the dead, and the soldiers who had entered and left the lane, each on separate lists.

Toward dawn, at last, the fires of Chang’an were cut off from one another. The daughter-in-law of old Liu the blacksmith soaked the felt she had prepared and threw it over a burning beam at the neighboring door. The old smith swung his axe until the wooden shed behind the house broke apart. He pulled two neighboring children free, and only then discovered that half his own shopfront had burned away. He sat among the broken tiles, his face too black with soot for anyone to see the tears, and shouted at the clerk who came to register the damage. “You said you could protect us. Where’s my house?”

The clerk offered no comforting answer. He wrote down each article lost and asked about injuries. On hearing that no one had died, he still entered the rescue of the two children by Liu’s daughter-in-law into the record. When the Crown Prince came to the ward, he ordered old felts from the government granaries lent to families without roofs, and carpenters sent to repair the doors. Whatever the state treasury could not repay was to be recorded as money owed.

There was fresh blood beneath the palace gate. As Fu Jian passed, a Xianbei soldier at his feet was binding the wound of a Di comrade. Both complained that the other was clumsy; neither let go of the other’s arm. Fu Jian watched them for a long time before asking how many had died the previous night. The keeper of records replied that the count was not yet complete. Bodies were still being identified ward by ward.

After morning, the first accounts of responsibility arrived at the Secretariat. Han Shou, the commander of Zhangcheng Gate, had fallen; Secretariat Registrar Zhang Chong had disappeared; the body believed to be that of the officer carrying the false relief order was burned beyond recognition. A Right Guard command token belonging to Yao Chang’s command had certainly appeared at Zhangcheng Gate, but the original duty-room register was missing. Other accounts of the fire, however, proved that Yao’s troops had rescued a substantial quantity of grain.

Fu Hong placed both sets of documents side by side before his father. He did not accuse Yao Chang of plotting the rebellion. He asked only that the arrangements for opening the city gates, the palace gates, and the Right Guard’s inner storehouse be changed. Fu Jian asked why. “The men who saved the imperial granary deserve credit,” his son replied. “What happened at Zhangcheng Gate still needs investigation. One act of service cannot settle a crime whose facts are not yet known.”

Later Yao Chang knelt before the hall and asked to be punished, saying that in the urgency of the night he had gone to fight the fire without first reporting to the throne. Fu Jian did not rebuke him. He ordered the palace gates placed under rotating detachments of the Left Guard, the Right Guard, and the central army. Yao remained commander of the Right Guard, but no longer held the keys or controlled the inner treasury by himself. He thanked the Heavenly King for his grace and withdrew. Palace servants passing nearby whispered that, without him the night before, His Majesty might have perished.

The same story spread through the streets. The Right Guard had saved grain; it had helped save the sovereign. Both things were true. Chang’an had not seen the expression on the rebel captain Fu Jian’s face when he died. People had seen only General Yao’s armor, black with smoke, and were willing to believe that he was a loyal hero. By that evening storytellers in the wine shops were already inventing tales of how he had ridden alone against the rebels. Murong Chui heard the stories and said nothing.

Fu Hong went to the room where the dead were laid out. Beside the charred body dressed as a Right Guard messenger lay an empty bronze tube. No one could say what it had once held. The Judicial Commandant asked whether the case should be closed by identifying the corpse as the messenger. The Crown Prince ordered the teeth, bones, and old injuries examined first. If the man could not be identified, the record was to say IDENTITY UNKNOWN. One dead man must not be used to wash every living suspect clean.

By nightfall the last pockets of fire had gone out. From the palace tower, Fu Jian looked north while the Crown Prince reported that Fu Luo’s main army was still advancing and that its vanguard had been almost destroyed. The new army was taking up positions by the Wei River bridge. Fu Jian said, “He knows I stayed. He will come.”

Fu Hong asked whether his father still wished to meet him. Fu Jian touched the damp rail, wet from the recent rain. “He brought his army to the north end of the bridge because he wants me to hear him out in person.”
“Will Father agree to his demands?”
“I have heard so many men speak, and still allowed them to die for nothing.” Fu Jian paused. “This time I must go myself.”

Not far beyond the palace, Han Shou’s body had been carried home. His mother found an amulet she had stitched for him when he was an infant and slipped it inside his uniform. She did not ask which people had wielded the knife that killed him. She asked only whether the gate he had guarded was securely shut now.
The servant told her it was.
